etymology: From where and on: on which. Webster 1828: on which. One of the compound relatives the Authorized Version uses in place of the looser modern which... on, and it carries the weight of two of the great holy-ground passages.
biblical_def: Twice a man is halted and told to take off his shoes, and both times the sentence turns on this word. At the bush: Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground (Exodus 3:5). And to Joshua before Jericho, from the captain of the LORD’s host: Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy. And Joshua did so (Joshua 5:15). Neither place was a sanctuary; the ground was holy because of who was standing on it, and the response required is the removal of what stands between the man and the dust. The word also carries a promise of inheritance, spoken over a fugitive sleeping on a stone: the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed (Genesis 28:13). And Rabshakeh uses it in the sharpest image of false confidence in the Old Testament: thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt; whereon if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it (Isaiah 36:6) — the support that wounds the hand that leans on it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WHEREON as on which, or on what; a compound relative and interrogative adverb formed from where and on.
webster_full: WHEREON, adv. — On which; as, the ground whereon he stood.
On what; as, whereon do ye lean?
Compare WHEREIN, in which; WHEREBY, by which; WHEREOF, of which.
These compounds were ordinary English in 1611 and remain the plainest way of joining a relative to its preposition.
From where, Anglo-Saxon hwaer, and on.
scriptures: Exodus 3:5
And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
Joshua 5:15
And the captain of the LORD'S host said unto Joshua, Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy. And Joshua did so.
Genesis 28:13
And, behold, the LORD stood above it, and said, I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac: the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed;
Isaiah 36:6
Lo, thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt; whereon if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all that trust in him.
corruption_summary: Exodus 3:5 locates holiness in God’s presence rather than in the place, which cuts against both the sacralizing of sites and the modern flattening that treats reverence as an outdated posture.
corruption_paragraphs: The ground at the bush had no history and no shrine; it was holy that morning because God was there, and Joshua’s field outside Jericho was the same. This is the principle the Reformation applied against the medieval traffic in holy places, relics and pilgrimage — holiness is not a property that adheres to soil, stone or bone, and cannot be accumulated by proximity to them. Our Lord states it to the Samaritan woman in as many words: neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, but in spirit and in truth (John 4:21-24). Yet the correction runs both ways. Because holiness is God’s presence and not the place, it is nearer rather than further, and the modern congregational manner — casual, chatty, indistinguishable from any other gathering — has drawn exactly the wrong conclusion from a true premise. Moses took his shoes off.

Isaiah 36:6 deserves separate notice because Rabshakeh, an unbeliever mocking Judah, happens to be right. Egypt was a broken reed, and leaning on it would pierce the hand. The passage is a standing warning against the political alliance that promises security and costs the soul, and Isaiah had already denounced the Egyptian treaty at length (Isaiah 30-31). The application is not that God’s people should avoid all lawful means — Scripture commends prudence and the use of second causes — but that the thing trusted determines the outcome. A reed will hold nothing and will wound the hand. The believer’s confidence rests where Isaiah puts it in the same book: in the LORD, in whom is everlasting strength.
roots_summary: Hebrew asher... alav, the relative with a preposition; Greek eph ho, upon which; hou (G3757), where; the English compound renders a construction both languages express with relative plus preposition.
roots_lines: Hebrew asher (H834) — the all-purpose relative particle, joined to a preposition to give the sense of whereon.
Hebrew adamath qodesh — holy ground; the ground made holy by the presence, not by its own history (Exodus 3:5).
Hebrew shakab (H7901) — to lie down; the land whereon thou liest (Genesis 28:13).
Hebrew qaneh ratsuts — a bruised or broken reed; Rabshakeh’s figure for Egypt (Isaiah 36:6).
Greek hou (G3757) — where, in which place; the New Testament counterpart of the Hebrew relative construction.
usage: The place whereon thou standest is holy ground (Exodus 3:5) — holy because of who is there, not because of what it is.
The land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it (Genesis 28:13) — a promise of inheritance to a fugitive asleep on a stone.
Whereon if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it (Isaiah 36:6) — the support that wounds the hand that leans.

etymology: From where and upon: upon which; in consequence of which. Webster 1828: upon which. In narrative it marks consequence, and Scripture uses it at two of the gravest hinges in redemptive history.
biblical_def: Whereupon is a hinge word: it announces that what follows is the consequence of what precedes. Hebrews uses it for the necessity of blood in the covenant: Whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood (Hebrews 9:18). The argument before it is that a testament is of force after men are dead; the conclusion is that not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood, and the chapter runs on to the better sacrifice. The word marks the exact opposite in Kings, where a king’s political calculation produces the sin that defines the northern kingdom for ever: Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel (1 Kings 12:28). Paul uses it of his own errand to Damascus: Whereupon as I went to Damascus with authority and commission from the chief priests (Acts 26:12). And God asks Job the question no one can answer: Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? or who laid the corner stone thereof (Job 38:6).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WHEREUPON as upon which; in consequence of which; hence, thereupon — marking that what follows results from what has just been stated.
webster_full: WHEREUPON, adv. — Upon which.
In consequence of which; hence; thereupon.
Upon what; as, whereupon do you ground this?
Compare THEREUPON, upon that; HEREUPON, upon this.
From where and upon.
scriptures: Hebrews 9:18
Whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood.
1 Kings 12:28

Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
Acts 26:12
Whereupon as I went to Damascus with authority and commission from the chief priests,
Job 38:6
Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? or who laid the corner stone thereof;
corruption_summary: Jeroboam’s calves were a convenience argument — Jerusalem is too far — and the sin that defined a kingdom for two centuries began as a reasonable adjustment to worship.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 12:28 repays close reading because the reasoning is so recognisable. Jeroboam does not renounce the LORD or import a foreign god; he addresses a practical problem (his people going up to a rival capital to worship) with a practical solution (two convenient sites and two visible aids), and he frames it pastorally: It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem. The verdict of Kings is that this became the sin of Jeroboam wherewith he made Israel to sin, repeated as an epitaph over king after king. The second commandment is not a technicality, and the regulative principle of worship — that what God has not commanded in worship is not permitted — exists precisely to prevent well-meant convenience from reshaping the ordinances. Every innovation in worship has been introduced by someone with a reason.

Hebrews 9:18 states the principle that governs the whole sacrificial system and therefore the cross: no covenant inauguration without blood, and, as the same chapter concludes, without shedding of blood is no remission (Hebrews 9:22). This is the point at which the modern discomfort with a bloody atonement becomes a doctrinal position rather than a matter of taste. Where penal substitution is set aside as primitive, the letter to the Hebrews becomes unusable, since its entire argument is that Christ’s blood accomplishes really what the first testament’s blood accomplished in figure. Job 38:6 supplies the posture appropriate to all such questioning: the foundations were laid by Someone, and it was not us.
roots_summary: Greek hothen (G3606), whence, wherefore; epi (G1909) with the relative, upon which; Hebrew al ken, upon which, therefore.
roots_lines: Greek hothen (G3606) — whence, from which, and so whereupon; the connective of Hebrews 9:18.
Greek en hois — in which circumstances; the construction rendered whereupon in Acts 26:12.
Hebrew al mah — upon what; the question put to Job about the foundations (Job 38:6).
Hebrew eden (H134) — a socket or base; the foundations whose fastening Job cannot explain.
Hebrew egel (H5695) — a calf; the two of gold that defined the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:28).
usage: Whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood (Hebrews 9:18) — the consequence on which the whole argument of Hebrews turns.
Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold (1 Kings 12:28) — a defining apostasy that began as a convenience.
Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? (Job 38:6) — the question that ends all questioning.

etymology: From whom, so and ever: whatever person, without restriction. Webster 1828: any person whatever. In the book of Daniel it is the word on which the doctrine of God’s rule over kingdoms turns.
biblical_def: Twice in one chapter, and both times as the lesson Nebuchadnezzar must learn by losing his reason, Daniel states the government of the world: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men (Daniel 4:17), and again, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will (Daniel 4:25). The clause is unqualified. Not permits, not influences — giveth it to whomsoever he will, and the appended phrase about setting up the basest of men forecloses the objection that God only gives thrones to the deserving. Our Lord uses the same word of the sovereign disclosure of the Father: no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him (Matthew 11:27). Knowledge of God is a gift in the Son’s giving. Even the devil, offering the kingdoms of the world, borrows the construction: to whomsoever I will I give it (Luke 4:6) — a claim the Lord does not stop to dispute, because Daniel has already settled whose it is.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WHOMSOEVER as the objective case of whosoever — any person whatever; whatever person, without limitation or exception.
webster_full: WHOMSOEVER, pron. — The objective case of whosoever.
Any person whatever; whatever person.
Compare WHOSOEVER, whatever person; WHATSOEVER, whatever thing.
The -soever ending generalizes without exception, and is one of the marks of the Authorized Version’s precision.
From whom, so, and ever.
scriptures: Daniel 4:17

This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men.
Daniel 4:25

That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.
Matthew 11:27
All things are delivered unto me of my Father: and no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him.
Luke 4:6
And the devil said unto him, All this power will I give thee, and the glory of them: for that is delivered unto me; and to whomsoever I will I give it.
corruption_summary: Daniel 4 states God’s absolute disposal of thrones without a qualifying clause, and Matthew 11:27 states the same absoluteness about the knowledge of God — both are routinely softened into permission.
corruption_paragraphs: The most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. The sentence has no escape hatch, and Daniel adds the hardest part: and setteth up over it the basest of men. God’s government of history is not confined to the rise of good rulers, and any doctrine of providence that quietly restricts it to what we would have chosen has stopped reading mid-verse. Romans 13:1 states the same thing for the New Testament church living under Nero: there is no power but of God, the powers that be are ordained of God. This does not sanctify what wicked rulers do — Scripture judges them without hesitation, and the doctrine of the lesser magistrate provides for lawful resistance — but it denies that any throne is held outside God’s disposal. Nebuchadnezzar had to lose his reason to learn it, and the text says he was restored the moment he lifted his eyes to heaven.

Matthew 11:27 applies the same unqualified sovereignty to the knowledge of God, and it is the harder of the two for the modern hearer. No man knows the Father save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him. Knowledge of God is not the achievement of the seeker but the gift of the Revealer, which is the doctrine of effectual calling stated by Christ Himself — and it stands immediately before the freest invitation in the Gospels, Come unto me, all ye that labour. Scripture sets sovereign election and universal invitation side by side in adjoining verses without embarrassment, and the systems that must remove one to keep the other — whether by making election conditional on foreseen faith or by muting the free offer — are tidier than the text.
roots_summary: Aramaic man di, whoever; Greek hos ean and hos an, whoever, whomsoever; the -soever ending renders the generalizing particle in both languages.
roots_lines: Aramaic man di yitsbe — whom he will; the clause of Daniel 4:17 and 4:25, unqualified in the original.
Aramaic illay (H5943) — the Most High; the title under which God’s rule over kingdoms is asserted in Daniel 4.
Greek hos ean — whoever, whomsoever; the generalizing relative of Matthew 11:27 and Luke 4:6.
Greek apokalupto (G601) — to uncover, to reveal; the Son’s act in Matthew 11:27.
Greek boulomai (G1014) — to will, to purpose; the verb of the Son’s sovereign choice in the same verse.
usage: Giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men (Daniel 4:17) — the clause has no escape hatch.
He to whomsoever the Son will reveal him (Matthew 11:27) — knowledge of God is a gift in the Son’s giving.
To whomsoever I will I give it (Luke 4:6) — even the tempter borrows the construction; Daniel has settled whose it is.

etymology: From where, so and ever: in whatever place, without restriction. Webster 1828: in whatever place. Our Lord uses it for a proverb of judgment and for a promise about a woman’s memorial.
biblical_def: In the Olivet Discourse, asked where, our Lord answers with a proverb rather than a map: For wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together (Matthew 24:28). The disciples want a location; He gives a principle — judgment finds its object as surely as carrion birds find a body, and no place needs naming. The same word carries one of the tenderest promises in the Gospels. When the disciples rebuked the woman for the ointment, Christ answered: Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her (Mark 14:9). It is a startling thing to attach to the gospel’s worldwide preaching — and it has been kept, since the passage is read wherever the gospel goes. Mark uses the companion form for the ordinary traffic of mercy: whithersoever he entered, into villages, or cities, or country, they laid the sick in the streets (Mark 6:56). And Luke records the disciples’ question and the same answer: Wheresoever the body is, thither will the eagles be gathered together (Luke 17:37).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WHERESOEVER as in what place soever; in whatever place; wherever, without limitation of place.
webster_full: WHERESOEVER, adv. — In what place soever; in whatever place.
Wherever; in any place at all.
Compare WHITHERSOEVER, to whatever place; WHENCESOEVER, from whatever place.
The -soever forms generalize absolutely, admitting no exception of place, person or thing.
From where, so, and ever.
scriptures: Matthew 24:28
For wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together.
Mark 14:9
Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her.
Mark 6:56

And whithersoever he entered, into villages, or cities, or country, they laid the sick in the streets, and besought him that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment: and as many as touched him were made whole.
Luke 17:37
And they answered and said unto him, Where, Lord? And he said unto them, Wheresoever the body is, thither will the eagles be gathered together.
corruption_summary: Christ answers a request for the where of judgment with a proverb rather than a location, which is a rebuke to the whole enterprise of mapping prophecy onto current geography.
corruption_paragraphs: Where, Lord? is the disciples’ question in Luke 17:37, and the answer is deliberately unlocalized: wherever the body is, there the eagles gather. Judgment does not need to be plotted; it finds its object. This is a standing check on the prophecy industry that assigns nations, rivers and modern armies to symbols and produces a new map with each generation’s headlines — an enterprise inseparable from the dispensational system this dictionary rejects as a nineteenth-century novelty (Darby, Scofield) absent from every Reformation confession. The millennial question itself remains open here among the historic positions; what is not open is the habit of treating our Lord’s deliberate refusal to give a location as though it were an invitation to supply one.

Mark 14:9 is worth setting beside it as the same word turned to mercy. A woman is criticized for waste, and Christ attaches her act to the gospel’s worldwide preaching for a memorial. Two things follow. The first is that Christ, not the onlookers, determines what counts as waste; the disciples had a defensible argument about the poor and were told to let her alone. The second is quieter: the promise has plainly been kept, and its keeping is a small standing evidence of the truth of the One who made it. Note also who receives the honour — not one of the Twelve, but a woman whose name Mark does not even record in this account, commended for extravagance toward Christ.
roots_summary: Greek hopou ean, wherever; hopou an, in whatever place; ptoma (G4430), a fallen body or carcase; aetos (G105), an eagle or vulture.
roots_lines: Greek hopou ean — wherever, in whatever place; the generalizing construction of Matthew 24:28 and Mark 14:9.
Greek ptoma (G4430) — a fallen thing, a corpse or carcase; the object the eagles find (Matthew 24:28).
Greek aetos (G105) — an eagle, and by usage a vulture; the bird of the proverb.
Greek mnemosunon (G3422) — a memorial, something that keeps a remembrance; Mark 14:9.
Greek hopou an with eisporeuomai — whithersoever he entered (Mark 6:56), the companion form of place to which.
usage: Wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together (Matthew 24:28) — a principle offered where a location was requested.
Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached... shall be spoken of for a memorial of her (Mark 14:9) — a promise plainly kept.
Whithersoever he entered... they laid the sick in the streets (Mark 6:56) — the ordinary traffic of mercy.

etymology: From there and unto: to that; to it. Webster 1828: to that; to this. Peter uses it twice for the Christian’s calling, and both times what he is called to is something no one would volunteer for.
biblical_def: Peter uses this word to attach a calling to a duty that runs against nature. Having forbidden retaliation he adds the ground: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing (1 Peter 3:9). The Christian does not merely refrain from returning insult; he blesses, and he does so because that is the thing he was called to. Paul uses it of affliction with the same finality: That no man should be moved by these afflictions: for yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto (1 Thessalonians 3:3). Afflictions are not an interruption to the appointment; they are the appointment. The word also fixes the manner of prayer to its object: Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints (Ephesians 6:18) — the last clause of the armour passage, and the one that makes the rest usable. Peter puts the same construction at the head of his great passage on Christ’s example: For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example (1 Peter 2:21).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines THEREUNTO as to that; to this — a compound adverb joining a verb to its object at a distance, and characteristic of the Authorized Version’s connective style.
webster_full: THEREUNTO, adv. — To that; to this.
Compare THEREUPON, upon that; THEREOF, of that; THEREIN, in that.
THEREUNTO is now archaic in speech but survives in legal English.
It renders a Greek relative-with-preposition compactly, keeping the antecedent clear.
From there and unto.
scriptures: 1 Peter 3:9
Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.
1 Thessalonians 3:3
That no man should be moved by these afflictions: for yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto.
Ephesians 6:18
Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints;
1 Peter 2:21
For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps:
corruption_summary: 1 Thessalonians 3:3 says believers are appointed to affliction, which is the plain denial of the teaching that suffering in a Christian’s life indicates a failure of faith.
corruption_paragraphs: We are appointed thereunto. Paul sends Timothy to Thessalonica specifically so that no one would be moved by the afflictions, and his stabilizing argument is not that the trouble will pass but that it was assigned. This is the flat contradiction of prosperity teaching, which must treat sustained affliction as evidence of insufficient faith, a hidden sin, or a failure to claim what is available. It also corrects a gentler error common among the orthodox — the assumption that a well-ordered Christian life should be largely free of trouble, so that trouble prompts the question what have I done wrong? Scripture’s answer is often nothing; Job’s comforters were rebuked for assuming otherwise. The 1689 Confession speaks of God leaving His children for a season to manifold temptations for holy ends, and Acts 14:22 tells the disciples plainly that through much tribulation we must enter into the kingdom.

1 Peter 3:9 is the harder command in practice. It is not enough to withhold the retort; the believer is to bless, and the reason given is that he was called to this. The therapeutic vocabulary now available for these situations — boundaries, toxicity, the duty to protect oneself — is not simply wrong about everything (Scripture knows about avoiding a foolish man and about lawful self-protection), but it supplies no category whatever for blessing the reviler, which is the actual apostolic command. Where that vocabulary becomes the church’s working ethic, 1 Peter 3:9 becomes unpreachable. And the ground Peter gives is not that blessing works, but that the blesser will inherit a blessing.
roots_summary: Greek eis touto, unto this; kaleo (G2564), to call; keimai (G2749), to be set or appointed; agrupneo (G69), to keep awake, to watch.
roots_lines: Greek eis touto — unto this, to that end; the phrase rendered thereunto and hereunto in Peter.
Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call; the calling to which the believer is thereunto called (1 Peter 3:9).
Greek keimai (G2749) — to lie, to be laid down or appointed; we are appointed thereunto (1 Thessalonians 3:3).
Greek agrupneo (G69) — to be sleepless, to keep watch; watching thereunto (Ephesians 6:18).
Greek hupogrammos (G5261) — a writing-copy set for a child to trace; the example Christ leaves (1 Peter 2:21).
usage: Ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing (1 Peter 3:9) — not merely withholding the retort, but blessing.
We are appointed thereunto (1 Thessalonians 3:3) — affliction is the appointment, not an interruption to it.
Watching thereunto with all perseverance (Ephesians 6:18) — the clause that makes the rest of the armour usable.

etymology: From all and though: grant that, admitting that. Webster 1828: grant all this; be it so; suppose that. Habakkuk uses it to build the greatest statement of faith without evidence in the Old Testament.
biblical_def: The last chapter of Habakkuk contains a sentence that has carried the church through every kind of loss, and its whole force rests on this conjunction: Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls (Habakkuk 3:17). Six clauses of total agricultural ruin — and then verse 18: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The prophet does not deny the ruin, minimize it, or expect it to be reversed; he grants the whole of it and rejoices anyway, in God rather than in circumstances. Jeremiah uses the word to make the covenant breach more painful, not less: which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD (Jeremiah 31:32) — the sentence that introduces the promise of the new covenant. And Exodus uses it of a route not taken: God led Israel not by the way of the Philistines, although that was near (Exodus 13:17), because the short road went past war.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ALTHOUGH as grant all this; be it so; allow all; suppose that; admitting that — a conjunction that concedes a fact and then sets a stronger fact against it.
webster_full: ALTHOUGH, conj. — Grant all this; be it so; allow all.
Suppose it to be so; admitting that; notwithstanding.
It concedes the truth of what follows it, and then subordinates it to the main clause.
Compare THOUGH, of the same force but weaker; NOTWITHSTANDING, of the same use.
From all and though; the all is intensive — grant it entirely.
scriptures: Habakkuk 3:17

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
Habakkuk 3:18
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
Jeremiah 31:32

Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD:
Exodus 13:17

And it came to pass, when Pharaoh had let the people go, that God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near; for God said, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt:
corruption_summary: Habakkuk 3:17-18 rejoices while granting the whole disaster, which is neither the denial that positive-confession teaching requires nor the resignation that fatalism produces.
corruption_paragraphs: Habakkuk does not confess the fig tree into blossom. He states the ruin in six clauses, refuses none of them, and then rejoices in the LORD — the joy is located in God, not in a reversal of circumstances he expects. This is fatal to the positive-confession teaching that treats the naming of a hard fact as an act of unbelief which helps to produce it; Scripture’s prophets name hard facts constantly and are commended for it. It is equally distant from stoic resignation, which manages the loss by lowering the value of what was lost. Habakkuk does neither. He grants that the loss is total and real, and rejoices in a God who is neither the loss nor the compensation for it. The verse following supplies the ground: The LORD God is my strength.

Exodus 13:17 shows the conjunction doing quieter work, and it is one of the most pastorally useful verses in the Pentateuch. God did not lead Israel by the near way although that was near, because the short road ran past war they were not ready for. The nearest route is not always the appointed one, and the reason given is mercy toward a people God knew would turn back. This is the doctrine of providence at the level of a road: God’s ordering of means takes account of what His people can bear, which is exactly what 1 Corinthians 10:13 promises. Any account of guidance that assumes the shortest and most obvious path must be the right one has not read the verse.
roots_summary: Hebrew ki (H3588), a versatile particle rendered although, for, when; im (H518), if, though; Greek kaiper (G2539), although, and yet.
roots_lines: Hebrew ki (H3588) — a particle of wide range, here concessive: although the fig tree shall not blossom (Habakkuk 3:17).
Hebrew asher (H834) — the relative, used concessively; although I was an husband unto them (Jeremiah 31:32).
Hebrew baal (H1166) — to be master or husband; the covenant relation Israel broke (Jeremiah 31:32).
Greek kaiper (G2539) — although, and yet; the New Testament concessive, used of Christ in Hebrews 5:8.
Hebrew alaz (H5937) — to exult, to rejoice; Habakkuk’s answering verb in 3:18.
usage: Although the fig tree shall not blossom... yet I will rejoice in the LORD (Habakkuk 3:17-18) — the ruin granted in full, and joy located in God.
Which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them (Jeremiah 31:32) — the concession that makes the breach worse.
God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near (Exodus 13:17) — the nearest road is not always the appointed one.

etymology: From further and more: moreover; besides; in addition. Webster 1828: moreover; besides; in addition to what has been said. In the epistles it marks the turn from argument to exhortation.
biblical_def: Furthermore is a hinge in the apostolic method: doctrine has been laid down, and now the duty is drawn from it. Hebrews uses it to move from the fact of chastening to its argument from lesser to greater: Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us, and we gave them reverence: shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live? (Hebrews 12:9). If a man honoured an earthly father who corrected him imperfectly and for a few years, the conclusion about the heavenly Father is not in doubt. Paul uses it to begin the practical half of an epistle: Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more (1 Thessalonians 4:1). Note that the exhortation is to abound in what they were already doing, not to correct a failure. In the prophets the word introduces a fresh and worse disclosure: He said furthermore unto me, Son of man, seest thou what they do? even the great abominations that the house of Israel committeth here (Ezekiel 8:6) — and the chapter goes on to greater abominations still.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FURTHERMORE as moreover; besides; in addition to what has been said — used to introduce a further point in the same argument.
webster_full: FURTHERMORE, adv. — Moreover; besides; in addition to what has been said.
It introduces an additional consideration bearing on the same matter.
FURTHER, a. — More distant; additional; as, a further inquiry.
FURTHER, v.t. — To help forward; to promote; to advance.
From further, the comparative of forth, and more.
scriptures: Hebrews 12:9
Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us, and we gave them reverence: shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live?
1 Thessalonians 4:1
Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more.
Ezekiel 8:6

He said furthermore unto me, Son of man, seest thou what they do? even the great abominations that the house of Israel committeth here, that I should go far off from my sanctuary? but turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations.
Hebrews 12:11
Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
corruption_summary: Hebrews 12 argues from fatherly correction to God’s dealings with His children, which a culture that has largely abandoned the category of loving correction can no longer hear as comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: The writer’s argument assumes something his readers took for granted: that a father who corrects his son does so out of love, and that the son who receives it gives him reverence. Where that assumption has collapsed — and it has collapsed widely, partly through real paternal failure and partly through a therapeutic account that reads correction itself as harm — Hebrews 12 stops sounding like comfort and starts sounding like a threat. But the chapter is written to console: chastening is the proof of sonship, and its absence would be the alarming thing (Hebrews 12:8). The remedy is not to soften the text but to recover the category, which is a matter for Christian fathers as much as for preachers. The fifth commandment and the biblical pattern of household order stand behind the argument, and where they are lost the argument cannot land.

1 Thessalonians 4:1 is a model of apostolic exhortation and a rebuke to a common pulpit habit. Paul is writing to a church that was already walking to please God, and his charge is that they abound more and more in it. He does not manufacture a deficiency to justify the sermon. Much preaching addresses congregations as though the assumed condition were failure, which over time trains hearers to receive every exhortation as an accusation and eventually to stop hearing it. Scripture’s pattern is to commend what is real, name what is lacking when it is lacking, and press growth on both. The Puritans, whose reputation for severity is largely a caricature, were careful about exactly this distinction between the sins of the saints and the state of the unconverted.
roots_summary: Greek eita (G1534), then, moreover; loipon (G3063), for the rest, furthermore; Hebrew od (H5750), yet, still, again.
roots_lines: Greek eita (G1534) — then, moreover; the connective opening Hebrews 12:9.
Greek loipon (G3063) — as for the rest, finally, furthermore; Paul’s turn to exhortation in 1 Thessalonians 4:1.
Hebrew od (H5750) — yet, still, again; he said furthermore unto me (Ezekiel 8:6).
Greek paideuo (G3811) — to train a child, to chasten; the fatherly correction of Hebrews 12.
Greek perisseuo (G4052) — to abound, to overflow; abound more and more (1 Thessalonians 4:1).
usage: Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us (Hebrews 12:9) — the argument from lesser to greater.
So ye would abound more and more (1 Thessalonians 4:1) — exhortation built on a commendation, not on a manufactured deficiency.
He said furthermore unto me... thou shalt see greater abominations (Ezekiel 8:6) — each disclosure worse than the last.

etymology: From where and to: to which; to what end. Webster 1828: to which; to what. Isaiah uses it for the errand on which God sends His word, and Paul for the point a believer has already reached.
biblical_def: The great promise about the effectiveness of God’s word turns on this word, and the promise is about an errand rather than a result in general: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it (Isaiah 55:11). The word is not guaranteed to do whatever the preacher hoped; it is guaranteed to accomplish what God sent it to do, which in the same chapter includes hardening as well as blessing. Paul uses it of the ground already gained: Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing (Philippians 3:16). Christians will not all be at the same point, and Paul’s rule is that each walk by what he has been given rather than dispute about the rest. He uses it again in one of the New Testament’s most compact statements of conversion: ye have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you (Romans 6:17). Job uses it in bitter interrogation: whereto might the strength of their hands profit me, in whom old age was perished? (Job 30:2).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WHERETO as to which; to what; and in older usage, to what end or purpose.
webster_full: WHERETO, adv. — To which; as, the end whereto he was appointed.
To what; to what end; as, whereto serveth this?
Compare WHEREUNTO, of the same sense and more frequent in the Authorized Version.
Compare WHEREFORE, for which cause; WHEREBY, by which means.
From where and to.
scriptures: Isaiah 55:11
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Philippians 3:16
Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing.
Romans 6:17
But God be thanked, that ye were the servants of sin, but ye have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you.
Job 30:2
Yea, whereto might the strength of their hands profit me, in whom old age was perished?
corruption_summary: Isaiah 55:11 promises that God’s word accomplishes God’s purpose, not the preacher’s, and it is commonly quoted as though it guaranteed visible success for every sermon.
corruption_paragraphs: It shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it. The guarantee is tied to God’s errand, and Isaiah’s own commission earlier in the book shows how wide that errand runs: he is sent to a people whose ears will be made heavy and whose eyes will be shut (Isaiah 6:9-10), and our Lord applies the same passage to His own hearers. The word never returns void, but its non-void effect may be hardening as truly as saving — Paul says the gospel is a savour of death unto death in them that perish and of life unto life in them that are saved (2 Corinthians 2:15-16). Preachers who quote Isaiah 55:11 to guarantee visible fruit have narrowed the promise and set themselves up for a discouragement the text does not require. The faithful man’s comfort is that the errand is God’s and the accomplishment is certain, whatever he can see of it.

Philippians 3:16 is a rule for peace among believers who are not at the same place, and it is easy to abuse in either direction. Paul has just said he does not count himself to have apprehended, and he allows that God will reveal to some what they do not yet see; his instruction is that each walk by what he has attained rather than break fellowship over the remainder. That is not a warrant for doctrinal indifference — the same epistle is fierce about the concision and about enemies of the cross, and the same apostle wrote Galatians. The distinction is the one the Reformers made between fundamental articles and matters of lesser weight, and keeping it is the difference between a church that can hold together and a movement that fractures over every disagreement.
roots_summary: Hebrew asher... lo, that to which; tsalach (H6743), to prosper or succeed; Greek eis ho, unto which; phthano (G5348), to arrive at, to attain.
roots_lines: Hebrew asher shalach — that to which He sent it; the errand clause of Isaiah 55:11.
Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to push forward, to prosper, to succeed in a purpose (Isaiah 55:11).
Hebrew reyqam (H7387) — empty, void, without effect; what the word shall not be.
Greek phthano (G5348) — to arrive at, to attain; whereto we have already attained (Philippians 3:16).
Greek tupos (G5179) — a form, mould or pattern; the form of doctrine delivered in Romans 6:17.
usage: It shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it (Isaiah 55:11) — the guarantee is tied to God’s errand, not the preacher’s hope.
Whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule (Philippians 3:16) — a rule for believers not at the same place.
That form of doctrine which was delivered you (Romans 6:17) — the mould into which the converted are poured.

etymology: From thence and forth: from that time onward. Webster 1828: from that time. It marks a boundary after which a thing is permanently different, and our Lord uses it of salt that has lost its savour.
biblical_def: The word draws a line that does not move. Our Lord uses it of a disciple who has lost the thing that made him useful: Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men (Matthew 5:13). The severity is in that one adverb. Salt without savour is not diminished salt; it is thenceforth good for nothing at all, and the only remaining use is the road. The Levitical law uses it for the point at which an animal becomes acceptable: from the eighth day and thenceforth it shall be accepted for an offering made by fire unto the LORD (Leviticus 22:27) — before that day, not acceptable; after it, acceptable. God’s appointments have thresholds. Chronicles marks the turn in Hezekiah’s standing after the deliverance from Sennacherib: so that he was magnified in the sight of all nations from thenceforth (2 Chronicles 32:23). And John records the exact point at which Pilate’s resistance began and, in the next breath, why it failed: And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend (John 19:12).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines THENCEFORTH as from that time; from that time forward — marking the beginning of a new and continuing condition.
webster_full: THENCEFORTH, adv. — From that time.
From that time forward; thereafter continually.
THENCEFORWARD, adv. — From that time onward; of the same force.
THENCE, adv. — From that place; from that time; for that reason.
From thence, Anglo-Saxon thanon, and forth.
scriptures: Matthew 5:13
Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.
Leviticus 22:27

When a bullock, or a sheep, or a goat, is brought forth, then it shall be seven days under the dam; and from the eighth day and thenceforth it shall be accepted for an offering made by fire unto the LORD.
2 Chronicles 32:23
And many brought gifts unto the LORD to Jerusalem, and presents to Hezekiah king of Judah: so that he was magnified in the sight of all nations from thenceforth.
John 19:12
And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend: whosoever maketh himself a king speaketh against Caesar.
corruption_summary: Matthew 5:13 says savourless salt is thenceforth good for nothing, which is not a threat of lost salvation but a warning that a church indistinguishable from the world has forfeited the only use it had.
corruption_paragraphs: Salt preserves and it stings; those are the two things it does, and both depend on its being unlike what it is put into. A church that sets out to become indistinguishable from the surrounding culture — in its ethics, its vocabulary, its estimate of what is shameful — has not become more useful to that culture but less, and Christ’s verdict is that it is thenceforth good for nothing but to be trodden under foot. The strategy of relevance has this exactly backwards: what the world needs from the church is precisely what the church is tempted to file off. Nor is this a warning aimed only at obviously liberal denominations; the same savourlessness arrives wherever a congregation’s distinctives are quietly retired to avoid friction. The passage is not teaching that a regenerate man can lose his salvation — the dictionary holds perseverance of the saints — but that a profession which no longer differs is a profession good for nothing.

Leviticus 22:27 is a small verse with a large principle: God appoints thresholds, and before the threshold the offering is simply not accepted. Seven days under the dam, and from the eighth day it may be brought. Nothing about the animal changes on the eighth morning except that God has said so, which is the whole point — acceptability is determined by God’s appointment and not by the worshipper’s estimate of sufficiency. This is the regulative principle in seed form, and it is the same logic that governs the ordinances of the New Testament church. John 19:12 shows what happens to a man who sees the right course and is governed by what a crowd may say of him: from thenceforth Pilate sought to release Him, and did not.
roots_summary: Greek eti and ek toutou, from this point; Hebrew halah (H1973), onward, thenceforth; maalah, upward and onward in time.
roots_lines: Greek ek toutou — from this, thenceforth; the turn in Pilate’s conduct (John 19:12).
Greek eti (G2089) — yet, still, any longer; the force of thenceforth good for nothing (Matthew 5:13).
Hebrew halah (H1973) — onward, further, thenceforth; from the eighth day and thenceforth (Leviticus 22:27).
Greek moraino (G3471) — to make foolish or insipid; the losing of savour in Matthew 5:13.
Hebrew ratsah (H7521) — to be pleased with, to accept favourably; the acceptance granted from the eighth day.
usage: It is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out (Matthew 5:13) — savourless salt is not diminished salt; it is useless salt.
From the eighth day and thenceforth it shall be accepted (Leviticus 22:27) — God appoints thresholds, and they are not negotiable.
And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him (John 19:12) — he saw the right course and was governed by the crowd.

etymology: From Old French refrener, from Latin refrenare, to bridle back, from re- and frenum, a bridle. Webster 1828: to hold back; to restrain; to keep from action. The image under the word is a bit in the mouth, and Scripture applies it first of all to the tongue.
biblical_def: The metaphor is a bridle, and Scripture puts it on the mouth. Peter quotes the Psalter for the plainest recipe for a good life in the New Testament: he that will love life, and see good days, let him refrain his tongue from evil, and his lips that they speak no guile (1 Peter 3:10). Proverbs states the same by arithmetic: In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise (Proverbs 10:19) — the more words, the more sin, and wisdom is fewer of them. Job, in the middle of his suffering, deliberately refuses the restraint and says so: Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul (Job 7:11). Scripture records the refusal without immediately condemning it, and God’s eventual answer to Job is not that he should have said nothing. The word is also used of God restraining Himself: For my name's sake will I defer mine anger, and for my praise will I refrain for thee, that I cut thee not off (Isaiah 48:9). And Gamaliel gives the counsel that saved the apostles: Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought (Acts 5:38).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REFRAIN as to hold back; to restrain; to keep from action; and intransitively, to forbear; to abstain; to keep one’s self from action or interference.
webster_full: REFRAIN, v.t. — To hold back; to restrain; to keep from action.
To forbear; to abstain from; as, to refrain the tongue.
REFRAIN, v.i. — To forbear; to abstain; to keep one’s self from action or interference.
REFRAINED, pp. — Held back; restrained.
Latin refrenare, from re, back, and frenum, a bridle — literally to rein in.
scriptures: 1 Peter 3:10
For he that will love life, and see good days, let him refrain his tongue from evil, and his lips that they speak no guile:
Proverbs 10:19
In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
Job 7:11
Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Acts 5:38
And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought:
corruption_summary: Proverbs 10:19 says plainly that more words means more sin, which is the standing judgment on an age that has made unrestrained expression a virtue and silence a symptom.
corruption_paragraphs: In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin. The proverb is arithmetical and it has no exceptions clause: increase the volume of speech and you increase the quantity of sin, because a fallen tongue discharges what a fallen heart contains. This is the reverse of the reigning assumption, in which expression is treated as intrinsically healthy, restraint as repression, and the unsaid thing as a burden that must be got out. Scripture knows a place for honest speech — the Psalms are full of it, and Job is about to prove it — but it never treats speech as self-justifying. James 1:19 gives the proportion: swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath. The bridle in the etymology is the right picture: a bridle does not silence a horse, it governs one.

Job 7:11 must be kept beside the proverb or the doctrine becomes cruelty. Job announces that he will not refrain, and pours out anguish and bitterness for many chapters. God’s final answer rebukes his presumption in questioning divine government, but God also says to Eliphaz that Job spoke of Him the thing that was right, and the comforters did not (Job 42:7). The lesson is that complaint addressed to God within the covenant is not the same as murmuring against Him, and the Psalter’s laments make the same distinction. Preaching that uses Proverbs 10:19 to silence a suffering saint has taken a proverb about the multiplication of sin and used it to forbid the very thing Scripture provides a whole genre for.
roots_summary: Hebrew chasak (H2820), to withhold or restrain; aphaq (H662), to hold in, to force oneself; Greek pauo (G3973), to cause to cease; aphistemi (G868), to stand off from.

Hebrew aphaq (H662) — to hold in, to force oneself; Joseph could not refrain himself (Genesis 45:1).
Hebrew chatam (H2413) — to muzzle or restrain; for my praise will I refrain for thee (Isaiah 48:9).
Greek pauo (G3973) — to make to cease; let him refrain his tongue from evil (1 Peter 3:10).
Greek aphistemi (G868) — to withdraw or stand away from; Gamaliel’s counsel (Acts 5:38).
usage: Let him refrain his tongue from evil (1 Peter 3:10) — a bridle does not silence a horse; it governs one.
In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin (Proverbs 10:19) — the proverb is arithmetical and has no exceptions clause.
Therefore I will not refrain my mouth (Job 7:11) — and God later says Job spoke of Him the thing that was right.
